Welcome to vertical farming—a way of growing food that asks a surprisingly simple question: What if agriculture could build upward, just as cities do?

The idea is easy to picture. Instead of spreading crops across one large surface, we grow them on multiple levels. Ten growing layers can provide roughly ten times the cultivation surface within the same building footprint. That does not automatically mean ten times the harvest; plants still need space, equipment, and access. But it changes how we think about agricultural land.

Vertical farming can take several forms. Today, let’s focus on its most controlled version: crops grown in stacked layers inside buildings, where growers manage light, water, nutrients, temperature, and humidity.

To understand how this works, we first need to separate two things we usually associate: plants and soil.

For most crops, soil provides support, water, oxygen around the roots, and essential minerals. But plants can obtain those things in other ways.

In hydroponics, roots receive water containing dissolved nutrients. In aeroponics, roots hang in the air and receive a nutrient-rich mist.

Think of soil as a pantry. Conventional farming relies on the pantry to supply what a plant needs. These systems deliver the ingredients directly.

Light is the other essential ingredient.

Through photosynthesis, plants use light energy to turn water and carbon dioxide into sugars—the building materials and fuel for growth. In an indoor farm, LEDs provide that energy. Growers adjust the light’s intensity, timing, and colour spectrum to suit different crops and stages of development.

Sensors monitor conditions. Software helps growers adjust them. Some facilities use cameras to spot growth problems and robots to move trays or handle harvesting.

This does not eliminate the skill of farming. It gives farmers a different set of tools.

So why bring this technology into cities?

One reason is water.

According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, agriculture accounts for about 70 percent of global freshwater withdrawals. That makes the way we grow food central to the way we manage water.

In a recirculating indoor system, water that roots do not absorb can be collected and reused. Some well-designed systems report using around 90 percent less water than conventional field cultivation for comparable crops, although savings depend on the crop, climate, and comparison.

Some facilities also capture moisture that plants release into the air and return it to the system.

Imagine watering a garden, collecting much of the drainage and escaping moisture, and using that water again. That is the basic principle.

Another advantage is greater control over growing conditions.

Outdoor crops face droughts, floods, frost, and heat waves. Indoor farms can maintain more consistent conditions throughout the year, making harvest schedules more predictable.

They also offer possibilities for places with limited farmland: dense urban districts, dry regions, or communities facing short growing seasons.

Locating production near customers can shorten the time between harvest and sale. For delicate foods such as lettuce and basil, that can mean fresher produce and potentially less spoilage.

But proximity alone does not make food sustainable.

This is where the story becomes more interesting—and more demanding.

An indoor farm must pay for something an outdoor field receives freely: sunlight.

Electricity powers the lights. More electricity runs pumps, fans, cooling equipment, and dehumidifiers. Plants release water vapour as they grow, and managing that moisture takes energy.

So vertical farming often exchanges lower land and water use for higher electricity demand.

Whether that exchange benefits the climate depends heavily on how efficiently the farm operates and how its electricity is generated.

A widely used global analysis estimates that transport accounts for about 6 percent of food-system greenhouse gas emissions. That figure varies greatly by food and transport method, especially for airfreighted produce. But it gives us an important lesson: reducing food miles does not automatically compensate for an energy-intensive growing system.

“Local” tells us where food comes from. It does not tell us its entire environmental footprint.

Economics creates another boundary.

Buildings, lighting, climate equipment, maintenance, and skilled labour cost money. That helps explain why commercial vertical farms have concentrated on leafy greens, herbs, and microgreens: crops that grow quickly, remain relatively compact, and can command higher prices.

Wheat, rice, and maize present a much harder business case. They are inexpensive sources of calories, and growing them indoors under electric lights is generally difficult to justify economically.

A city could grow more of its salad indoors. Supplying its staple calories is a very different challenge.

The useful question, then, is where vertical farming fits within a broader food system.

It could supply fresh greens near consumers, support plant breeding and seedling production, or provide additional growing capacity where land and water are scarce. Alongside it, cities can support community gardens, rooftop farms, greenhouses, and strong connections with surrounding rural farms.

Each approach has strengths. Resilience comes partly from having several options.

The future will depend on practical improvements: more efficient lighting, crops suited to indoor conditions, cleaner electricity, better climate control, and business models that can deliver affordable food.

We should judge progress by measurable results: water used per kilogram harvested, electricity consumed, emissions produced, food wasted, and prices people can actually afford.

When you next pass an empty urban building, imagine those shelves of growing plants.

Then look beyond the glow. Consider the water circulating through the roots, the electricity entering the building, and the people who will buy the harvest.
